intro: Every day, people buy and sell things. A family buys milk. A kid sells lemonade. A farmer sells corn. Each time, someone has to decide on a price. Why is a cup of lemonade 50 cents one day and 75 cents the next? This unit helps you find out.

You will also follow money on its trip. You will see why people stopped trading apples for shoes and started using coins and bills. You will visit a bank, see what it does with your savings, and learn how interest makes money grow.

By the end, you will be able to explain why prices go up and down. You will be able to figure out simple interest. And you will be able to make a budget for your own money, with a plan to spend, save and share.
bigQuestion: How do buyers, sellers and banks work together to set prices and put money to work?

test.q: The price of bananas goes down. What will shoppers most likely do?
test.why: The law of demand: when the price goes down, people buy more.

test.q: Bakers can now sell a pie for $15 instead of $10. What will bakers most likely do?
test.why: The law of supply: when the price goes up, sellers offer more.

test.q: A store has 5 bikes and 25 people want one. What is this?
test.why: More people want bikes than there are for sale. That is a shortage.

test.q: After a shortage, what usually happens to the price?
test.why: Buyers compete for the few items, so the price goes up.

test.q: A shop has 300 leftover beach towels in October. What will it most likely do?
test.why: This is a surplus. Sellers lower the price so more people buy.

test.q: A second bakery opens next to the first. What will likely happen to bread prices?
choices: They will go down or the bread will get better
test.why: Competition pushes sellers to offer lower prices or better quality.

test.q: At 30 cents, kids want 50 pencils and the store has 50. What is 30 cents?
test.why: The amount wanted equals the amount for sale. That is the market price, or equilibrium.

test.q: Gas prices jump. Some families ride bikes instead of driving. What is the high price doing?
choices: Sending a signal to buy less
test.why: A high price is a signal. It tells buyers to use less or find a substitute.

test.q: Tom has fish and wants bread. The baker wants eggs. Why is barter hard here?
choices: The baker does not want what Tom has
test.why: Barter only works when each person wants what the other has.

test.q: You keep $10 in a drawer to spend next month. Which job of money is this?
test.why: Saving money to use later is money's job as a store of value.

test.q: Eva deposits $60, withdraws $15, then deposits $20. How much is in her account?
Why does a bank pay interest to savers?
choices: The law says banks must give gifts
The bank uses their money to make loans
test.why: The bank pays savers for the use of their money, which it lends to borrowers.

test.q: Max saves $400 at 5% simple interest a year (example rate). How much interest does he earn in one year?
Rosa borrows $100 at 10% simple interest for one year (example rate). How much does she pay back?
Dev earns $20 a week. He plans $10 to spend and $6 to save. How much is left to share?

write.prompt: Your class runs a snack stand at the school fair. You have 100 bags of popcorn. At $1 a bag, you think 150 people will want one. At $2, about 100 people. (Made-up numbers.) What price should you charge? Then plan what the class should do with the money it earns: spend, save in a bank, or share. Explain your choices.
tips: Say whether each price makes a shortage, a surplus or neither
Show your math with the numbers
Name what you give up with each choice for the money
If you save in a bank, show how interest could help
